<h1>Earthship Biotecture in a Hot-Humid Climate</h1>
<div class="cover-rule"></div>
<div class="subtitle">
      A climate-adapted concept report for a single-family off-grid residence in Lafayette, Louisiana,
      integrating traditional Earthship principles with Gulf Coast enclosure design, psychrometric control,
      HVAC sizing, rainwater harvesting, and Louisiana-specific process flow diagrams.
    </div>
</div>
<div class="meta">
<strong>Prepared for:</strong> Matthew<br/>
<strong>Prepared by:</strong> ChatGPT<br/>
<strong>Date:</strong> April 22, 2026<br/>
<strong>Base case:</strong> 2,000 ft² single-family residence, 4 occupants, Lafayette, Louisiana<br/>
<strong>Document purpose:</strong> concept-level design basis and preliminary system sizing
  </div>
</section><main class="embed-main">
<section class="page-break">
<div class="eyebrow" style="color:#7a6d58;">Contents</div>
<div class="toc">

<h2 id="1-executive-summary">1. Executive summary</h2>
<p class="lead">
    Traditional Earthships were developed for dry, high-desert conditions where thermal mass, passive solar gain,
    and water scarcity dominate the design problem. Louisiana presents the opposite challenge: abundant rainfall,
    high dew points, flood risk, and persistent latent cooling loads.
  </p>
<p>
    This report reframes the Earthship not as a fixed desert template, but as a <strong>closed-loop habitation system</strong>
    whose principles can be adapted to a hot-humid climate. The proposed Louisiana Earthship keeps the core ideas of
    on-site power generation, rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse, food production, and reclaimed/local materials,
    but it replaces desert assumptions with Gulf Coast building science: a drained enclosure, a robust air-control layer,
    continuous exterior insulation, flood-aware foundation design, and dedicated humidity control.
  </p>
<p>
    The result is not a copy of a Taos Earthship. It is a <strong>climate-adapted Earthship variant</strong> for Lafayette:
    a 2,000 ft² single-family residence with rain-harvesting capability, a variable-speed heat pump, a dedicated
    whole-house dehumidifier, and a wall/roof assembly built around moisture control while still preserving the Earthship
    philosophy of mass, reuse, and local material use wherever practical.
  </p>
<h2 id="2-research-background-traditional-earthships">2. Research background: traditional Earthships</h2>
<p>
    Earthship Biotecture describes the Earthship as an integrated system that catches water from the roof into cisterns,
    pumps it through a <em>Water Organizing Module</em>, treats it for household use, and similarly packages the electrical side
    around a <em>Power Organizing Module</em> for off-grid generation and distribution. Those two organizing modules reflect the
    larger Earthship design idea: the dwelling is treated as a self-contained utility plant rather than a conventional house.
  </p>
<p>
    The traditional Earthship relies on six linked principles: passive solar heating/cooling, renewable electricity,
    contained sewage treatment, building with recycled and natural materials, rainwater harvesting, and food production.
    This model has clear resilience advantages, and recent research from Puerto Rico found that Earthship principles can align
    strongly with post-disaster independence goals. At the same time, that same humid-climate research also highlighted
    barriers such as moisture management, regulation, financing, and climate mismatch. Those barriers are precisely what
    this Louisiana report addresses.
  </p>
<div class="callout">
<strong>Design position used in this report:</strong> preserve the Earthship <em>systems philosophy</em>, not every
    geometric or material detail of the Taos prototype. In Louisiana, durability and humidity control must be treated as
    first-order engineering requirements.
  </div>
<h2 id="3-louisiana-climate-and-design-basis">3. Louisiana climate and design basis</h2>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Parameter</th><th>Base value</th><th>Design implication</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Location</td><td>Lafayette Parish, Louisiana</td><td>Hot-humid Gulf Coast climate</td></tr>
<tr><td>Cooling design temperature</td><td>94 °F (1%)</td><td>High summer sensible and latent load</td></tr>
<tr><td>Heating design temperature</td><td>32 °F (99%)</td><td>Modest winter heating need</td></tr>
<tr><td>Annual precipitation</td><td>62.64 in (30-year normal)</td><td>Rainwater viability improves; overflow and quality control become essential</td></tr>
<tr><td>Annual cooling degree days</td><td>2,954</td><td>Cooling season dominates annual HVAC operation</td></tr>
<tr><td>Dwelling size</td><td>2,000 ft², single-story</td><td>Single-family concept sizing basis</td></tr>
<tr><td>Occupancy</td><td>4 persons</td><td>Used for internal gains and water demand basis</td></tr>
<tr><td>Indoor target</td><td>75 °F, 50% RH</td><td>Comfort and mold-control target</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="small footer-note">
    Climate and design values above are concept-level basis values used for preliminary sizing and narrative design development.
  </div>
</section>
<section class="page-break">
<h2 id="4-psychrometric-analysis">4. Psychrometric analysis</h2>
<p>
    In Louisiana, the design problem is not only about dry-bulb temperature. It is about forcing outside air from a
    hot-wet state to a cooler-drier indoor condition without allowing the enclosure to condense moisture or the interior
    to drift into mold-supporting relative humidity.
  </p>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Air state</th><th>Dry-bulb</th><th>Relative humidity / wet-bulb</th><th>Humidity ratio</th><th>Enthalpy</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Outdoor design state</td><td>94 °F</td><td>Approx. 78 °F coincident wet-bulb</td><td>0.0167 lb/lb dry air (117 grains/lb)</td><td>41.0 Btu/lb dry air</td></tr>
<tr><td>Indoor target state</td><td>75 °F</td><td>50% RH</td><td>0.00921 lb/lb dry air (64.5 grains/lb)</td><td>28.1 Btu/lb dry air</td></tr>
<tr><td>Required air-side reduction</td><td>-19 °F</td><td>-</td><td>0.00753 lb/lb dry air (52.7 grains/lb)</td><td>12.9 Btu/lb dry air</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="calc">Interpretation:
- Every pound of infiltrating or ventilated outdoor air must lose roughly 53 grains of moisture before it reaches the indoor target.
- In a hot-humid climate, latent control remains significant even when sensible loads are reduced by shading, insulation, and airtightness.
- For this reason, passive cooling measures alone are not sufficient for a Louisiana Earthship occupied as a full-time residence.</div>
<h3>Outdoor air example</h3>
<p>
    At roughly 80 CFM of controlled outdoor ventilation, the outside air stream alone contributes a meaningful latent load
    in addition to its sensible load. This is why the mechanical concept in this report uses both a high-efficiency heat pump
    and a dedicated whole-house dehumidifier. The air conditioner cannot be treated as a temperature-only device.
  </p>
<h2 id="5-envelope-design-for-a-louisiana-earthship">5. Envelope design for a Louisiana Earthship</h2>
<p>
    The envelope strategy follows a simple rule from Building Science practice: <strong>control rain first, then air, then heat,
    while keeping the assembly able to dry</strong>. Traditional Earthships often depend on large exposed mass and substantial earth
    contact. In Louisiana, those choices increase moisture risk unless the control layers are reorganized.
  </p>
<h3>5.1 Recommended wall assembly</h3>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Preferred material strategy</th><th>Role</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Exterior cladding</td><td>Reclaimed cypress rainscreen or lime-based stucco</td><td>Bulk rain shedding and solar protection</td></tr>
<tr><td>Drainage cavity</td><td>3/4 in ventilated gap</td><td>Drainage and back-ventilation</td></tr>
<tr><td>Water / air control layer</td><td>Fluid-applied or sheet air barrier, vapor-open where possible</td><td>Primary rain and air control</td></tr>
<tr><td>Continuous insulation</td><td>2-3 in mineral wool or equivalent moisture-tolerant board</td><td>Thermal control; keeps mass warm enough to reduce condensation risk</td></tr>
<tr><td>Mass wall</td><td>Reclaimed brick, filled CMU, stabilized earth block, or earthbag hybrid</td><td>Structure + interior thermal ballast</td></tr>
<tr><td>Interior service cavity</td><td>1.5-3.5 in furring zone</td><td>Protects control layers and simplifies wiring/plumbing</td></tr>
<tr><td>Interior finish</td><td>Lime or clay-lime plaster</td><td>Durable finish with a material language consistent with Earthship construction</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="callout">
<strong>Why this arrangement matters:</strong> the mass wall remains inside the insulation instead of sitting directly behind
    the exterior weather exposure. That preserves the Earthship benefit of thermal mass while greatly improving moisture safety
    in a hot-humid climate.
  </div>
<h3>5.2 Foundation and earth contact</h3>
<p>
    A Louisiana Earthship should be <strong>raised</strong> rather than deeply bermed. Recommended options include an elevated slab or
    a pier-and-grade-beam system above finished grade and local flood exposure. This follows Gulf Coast durability logic and
    avoids turning the building into a moisture sink. Earth contact, if used at all, should be limited and aggressively detailed
    with drainage, capillary breaks, and inspection access.
  </p>
<h3>5.3 Roof assembly</h3>
<p>
    Because the roof is both the primary weather barrier and the rainwater collection surface, the roof should be a light-colored
    standing-seam metal assembly with deep overhangs, sealed penetrations, and a high-performance insulated roof section.
    A concept-level target of <strong>R-38 to R-49</strong> is appropriate for this house size and climate. The HVAC air handler and all
    ducts should remain inside conditioned space.
  </p>
<h3>5.4 South greenhouse adaptation</h3>
<p>
    A classic fully open greenhouse corridor is too humid for Louisiana if permanently connected to the main living zone.
    The adapted concept is a <strong>semi-decoupled solar porch / food-production zone</strong> with low-SHGC glazing, floor drainage,
    closable openings to the conditioned house, and strong seasonal control over ventilation and humidity migration.
  </p>
<div class="pfd-inline">
  <p class="pfd-intro">PFD-05 is placed here because envelope moisture control is the central redesign that makes the Earthship concept viable in Louisiana.</p>
  <div class="pfd-card full">
<img alt="PFD-05 Louisiana building envelope moisture control" src="data:image/png;base64,
"/>
<div class="pfd-cap"><strong>PFD-05.</strong> Building-envelope moisture-control concept for a hot-humid Louisiana Earthship.</div>
</div>
</div>

</section>
<section class="page-break">
<h2 id="6-hvac-concept-and-preliminary-sizing">6. HVAC concept and preliminary sizing</h2>
<p>
    For a 2,000 ft² single-family residence with the enclosure described above, low-SHGC glazing, shading, airtightness near
    1.5 ACH50, and controlled ventilation, a concept-level peak load estimate places the house in the range of a
    <strong>2.0 to 2.5 ton cooling system</strong>. Because latent load remains prominent, oversizing should be avoided.
  </p>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Load category</th><th>Concept-level range</th><th>Notes</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Sensible cooling</td><td>16,000 - 19,000 Btu/h</td><td>Controlled by enclosure, shading, glazing, and internal gains</td></tr>
<tr><td>Latent cooling</td><td>6,000 - 8,000 Btu/h</td><td>Driven by outdoor air, infiltration, occupants, and interior moisture sources</td></tr>
<tr><td>Total cooling</td><td>22,000 - 27,000 Btu/h</td><td>Supports a 2.0-2.5 ton variable-speed selection envelope</td></tr>
<tr><td>Heating</td><td>Modest</td><td>Handled by heat pump with electric backup only if required by final Manual J</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3>Recommended mechanical package</h3>
<table>
<thead><tr><th>System</th><th>Preliminary specification</th><th>Reason</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Primary HVAC</td><td>2.5 ton variable-speed ducted heat pump</td><td>Long runtimes improve moisture removal and comfort</td></tr>
<tr><td>Supplemental humidity control</td><td>70-90 pint/day whole-house dehumidifier</td><td>Independent latent control during mild but humid weather</td></tr>
<tr><td>Ventilation</td><td>70-90 CFM balanced fresh-air system / ERV logic as appropriate</td><td>Fresh air without surrendering humidity control</td></tr>
<tr><td>Distribution</td><td>All ducts and air handler inside conditioned envelope</td><td>Protects efficiency and reduces condensation risk</td></tr>
<tr><td>Controls</td><td>75 °F / 50-55% RH target with humidity-priority logic</td><td>Comfort plus mold-risk reduction</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="calc">Mechanical design note:
The original desert-style Earthship assumption that "HVAC can be omitted from the electrical design" is not appropriate here.
For a Louisiana residence, HVAC and dehumidification become major electrical loads and must be included in the final PV / battery sizing exercise.</div>
<div class="pfd-inline">
  <p class="pfd-intro">PFD-04 summarizes the hot-humid air handling loop: outdoor air, ventilation, cooling, dehumidification, supply, and return.</p>
  <div class="pfd-card">
<img alt="PFD-04 Louisiana HVAC and psychrometric control system" src="data:image/png;base64,"/>
<div class="pfd-cap"><strong>PFD-04.</strong> HVAC and psychrometric control loop for temperature and humidity management.</div>
</div>
</div>

<h2 id="7-water-wastewater-and-energy-implications">7. Water, wastewater, and energy implications</h2>
<h3>7.1 Rainwater opportunity</h3>
<p>
    Louisiana greatly improves the viability of the Earthship water concept. Using a 2,000 ft² catchment roof, 62.64 in/year of rainfall,
    and an 85% collection efficiency factor, annual harvested water is approximately:
  </p>
<div class="calc">Annual water yield ≈ 2,000 ft² × 62.64 in × 0.623 gal/(ft²·in) × 0.85
                  ≈ 66,300 gallons/year</div>
<p>
    That is substantially higher than the same roof in Taos-like conditions and can support a low-to-moderate demand household, especially
    if water is cascaded through greywater reuse and efficient fixtures. The key Louisiana additions are overflow handling, covered cisterns,
    mosquito-resistant vents, and robust filtration.
  </p>
<div class="pfd-inline">
  <p class="pfd-intro">PFD-02 is embedded with the rainwater section to show collection, first-flush diversion, storage, filtration, pressure delivery, and overflow management.</p>
  <div class="pfd-card">
<img alt="PFD-02 Louisiana rainwater harvesting and treatment system" src="data:image/png;base64,
"/>
<div class="pfd-cap"><strong>PFD-02.</strong> Rainwater harvesting, storage, treatment, and overflow control.</div>
</div>
</div>

<h3>7.2 Wastewater adaptation</h3>
<p>
    Traditional Earthships often rely heavily on indoor botanical cells. In Louisiana, most greywater treatment should move outdoors into
    planted treatment beds or wetlands so that interior humidity is not driven upward by open warm-water planters. A limited interior
    planting zone may still be used for educational or food-production value, but it should not carry the entire treatment burden.
  </p>
<div class="pfd-inline">
  <p class="pfd-intro">PFD-03 is embedded with wastewater because Louisiana shifts most biological treatment outdoors to reduce indoor humidity and mold risk.</p>
  <div class="pfd-card">
<img alt="PFD-03 Louisiana greywater and blackwater management system" src="data:image/png;base64,
"/>
<div class="pfd-cap"><strong>PFD-03.</strong> Greywater and blackwater management with outdoor treatment emphasis.</div>
</div>
</div>

<h3>7.3 Energy implication</h3>
<p>
    Once a Louisiana Earthship includes a variable-speed heat pump, dehumidifier, ventilation fan energy, and water pumping, the solar and
    battery system needs a fresh sizing study. The Louisiana adaptation therefore improves water feasibility but increases the electrical
    importance of HVAC.
  </p>
<div class="pfd-inline">
  <p class="pfd-intro">PFD-01 closes the systems section by showing the integrated power architecture, where HVAC and dehumidification become first-class electrical loads.</p>
  <div class="pfd-card">
<img alt="PFD-01 Louisiana solar and HVAC integrated microgrid" src="data:image/png;base64,
"/>
<div class="pfd-cap"><strong>PFD-01.</strong> Solar + HVAC integrated microgrid.</div>
</div>
</div>

</section>
<h2 id="8-conclusion">8. Conclusion</h2>
<p>
    The Earthship idea remains powerful in Louisiana, but only if it is translated rather than transplanted. The traditional model contributes
    the systems philosophy: catch and reuse water, harvest renewable energy, use mass and recycled materials, and treat the house as a
    resilient off-grid habitat. Louisiana contributes the constraints that force rigor: flood risk, high rainfall, persistent humidity,
    inward vapor drives, and large latent loads.
  </p>
<p>
    The resulting design is therefore best understood as a <strong>Louisiana Earthship variant</strong>: a high-mass, reclaimed-material,
    rain-harvesting residence that uses modern Gulf Coast enclosure practice and active humidity control to make the Earthship concept
    durable and habitable in a hot-humid climate.
  </p>
